text:
“And not from me, in any case?”

“From you? What do you mean, from you?”

“You once told me, while speaking to me of other things: ‘My family bores me; perhaps a day will come when I shall be free, entirely free, because I want to sing.’ Do you remember telling me that?”

“Yes, I remember, and I repeat: A day will come, perhaps soon, when I shall be free.”

“There, and thinking of that day, I too have had a dream... but one so beautiful that I do not dare tell you.”

“Dreams...” she said teasingly, “dreams have this good quality: they serve to tell things that are too difficult to say.”

“You are right, Loretta,” he admitted. “So, a dream. That I should get you a little villa, not too far from Villa Giuliani, small, for you alone. A secluded little villa, with a beautiful garden, an orchard, a stable. You would be free; no one would know who you are. Sometimes, so as not to remain alone, you would open the gate to me.”

“Ah... and that is the dream?”

“Yes, that is it.”

She reflected for a moment, then said:

“Go on.”

“What do you mean?”

“After the summer...”

“Well, after the summer you may choose whatever you please. In the autumn, for example, a lovely journey, a little escape by motorcar, if you like, even abroad, if you like... And in winter, your house in the city, a lady companion to preserve appearances, a teacher to teach you singing.”

“And in the spring,” she exclaimed, still tempted, “since the year blossoms anew, someone else is put in Lora’s place, and everything begins again: the same villa, the journey, the city house... No, thank you!”

“Someone else? What are you saying? Have you still not understood that I love you, that I have loved you for many months, more strongly every day? That you can make me obey like a child, and you alone, you alone, must give me back the peace I no longer have?... Someone else? That word makes no sense! But think for a moment. Do you believe I do not know what risks I am running by making you this proposal? Well, what do I care? I do not want to, I can no longer think! No danger frightens me. Only say yes! Ask me for whatever you want, but say yes!”

“I ask for nothing,” she said, regretting having let herself appear so calculating.

“Then listen, hear me...” And he knelt before her armchair and encircled her with his arms.

“What are you doing? What are you doing?”

“Nothing; I am begging you on my knees. Love me a little; be kind to me for once!”

Thus on his knees, leaning toward her in the ardor of his desire, with passionate eyes and a pleading voice, Rafa was almost handsome, and she looked at him.

“Come, leave me alone...” she said, with a certain annoyance.

He held her tightly around the waist and, leaning a little against her, covered her dress and her wrists with tiny kisses.

“How many mistresses have you had sit in this armchair?” she suddenly asked.

“How many? None.”

“Oh, come now! I am asking out of curiosity.”

“Perhaps,” he said, “some woman has come here, but I do not remember. They were not mistresses; they were not you. If you do not like it, we shall change houses. I had no love before meeting you. Now you seem the first to me. I love you, I love you in every way; you haunt me and you delight me. You are beautiful. You have such an indefinable grace that I suffer when I am near you. Be kind to me; do not laugh!...”

She was indeed laughing, but with a somewhat nervous laugh, and her mouth, her eyes, her hands were no longer so calm.

“No, leave me alone...” she pleaded. “Let me go, please... you are hurting me terribly...”

In the half-light he saw her turn pale; he hid his face in her lap and clasped her knees with his arms.

She tried to lift his burning forehead, tried to push away that importunate mouth, but, unable to overcome his strength, in sudden anger she thrust her convulsed fingers into his hair.

Then the struggle was brief: desperately, the girl closed her eyes and let herself be carried away...

But she saw another room, at night, with its windows open over a lake white with moonlight and the stars near, infinite; another man bent over her, covering her with caresses and kisses. And she saw herself again in that bed, and relived the agony of that vanished hour, and for an instant it seemed to her that he had returned, that he was there, on his knees, and was kissing her as terribly as he had then, and that his hands were running, feverish, burning, all over her inflamed body, and that a mouth was rising, rising to her lips, full of anguish, fever, voluptuousness, and terror...

A little later, it was dark in the adjoining room, and from room to room, throughout the silent house, the cry of her lost virginity was suddenly heard.




II


At about five in the afternoon, Beppe Cianella entered the Club and, after ordering an iced drink, sprawled indolently on a leather sofa near the small table where Gigi Saletta, nicknamed Saponetta, and several others were playing poker.

Beppe Cianella was hot and wiped his sweaty brow with a brightly colored silk handkerchief. He unbuttoned his waistcoat, lit a cigar, and blissfully closed his eyes as though about to doze off. But it was too hot to sleep. In a still-drowsy voice, Beppe Cianella called the servant and asked him to turn the fan toward him.

When the cool air struck him, he stretched out more comfortably on the sofa and, with a feeling of true bliss, tried to close his mischievous eyes.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair,” he said with a slight yawn.

“So much the better for him!” replied one of the players.

Sacco Berni had attempted a daring “bluff,” but Gigi Saponetta, an extremely skillful player, had forced him to declare his hand, and the others, laughing wildly over it, mocked the trickster who had been tricked.

Count Berrini passed by at the back, in his shirtsleeves, shouting at the servants because he could not find a newspaper; Lello Fornara, the languishing one, was writing his daily love letter in a corner; through the open door leading into the billiard room, the balls could be heard striking one another amid the noisy quarrels of old Baron Gioacchini and his young pupil Leonardo Sergi.

“Rafa Giuliani is having an affair!” Beppe Cianella, who could not fall asleep, repeated between one yawn and the next.
